title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Review

What is ridge regression minimizing, and what is \(\hat\beta^R\)?



RSS \(+ \lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j^2\), minimized by \((\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\).

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
What ridge cannot do

Ridge keeps all \(p\) predictors in the model at every finite \(\lambda\). On Credit that is ten coefficients to report when four of them carry the signal.



Subset selection drops predictors and ridge shrinks them. Is there something that does both?

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
The lasso
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_{ij}\right)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|\]

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
The lasso
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_{ij}\right)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$|\beta_j|$}}\]
The absolute value of one coefficient, where ridge had its square. That is the whole difference between the two methods.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
The lasso
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_{ij}\right)^2 + \lambda{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|$}}\]
Summed over the \(p\) predictors, this is the \(\ell_1\) norm \(\|\beta\|_1\), where ridge used the squared \(\ell_2\) norm \(\|\beta\|_2^2\). The sum starts at \(j = 1\), so the intercept goes unpenalized here too.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
The lasso
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_{ij}\right)^2 + {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\lambda$}}\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|\]
The same tuning parameter, chosen the same way, by cross-validation. At \(\lambda = 0\) this is least squares, and at \(\lambda\) large enough every coefficient is exactly zero.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Two norms


Ridge
\[\|\beta\|_2^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2\]
Shrinks every coefficient toward zero.

Lasso
\[\|\beta\|_1 = \sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|\]
Shrinks, and sets some to exactly zero.



A model with some coefficients exactly zero is called sparse. The lasso performs variable selection as a side effect of shrinking.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
The budget form


Lasso
minimize RSS subject to \[\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j| \leq s\]

Ridge
minimize RSS subject to \[\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2 \leq s\]



For every \(\lambda\) there is an \(s\) giving the same answer. Large \(\lambda\) is a small budget.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
The constraint regions


ISLP Figure 6.7. Contours of RSS in red against the constraint regions in blue: a diamond for the lasso on the left, a circle for ridge on the right.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Corners

The RSS contours grow outward from \(\hat\beta\) until they touch the constraint region. The diamond has corners on the axes, and a corner is a point where one coefficient is exactly zero.



A circle has no corners. Where does the ridge solution touch, and what does that mean for a coefficient reaching zero?

title: Lasso and elastic net
section: Best subset in the same picture
text:
Best subset in the same picture

Best subset selection is minimizing RSS subject to \(\sum_{j=1}^{p}I(\beta_j \neq 0) \leq s\): a budget on how many coefficients may be nonzero.



Same shape of problem, a budget that cannot be searched in reasonable time. The lasso replaces it with one that can.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Elastic net
\[\text{RSS} + \lambda\left(\alpha\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j| + (1-\alpha)\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2\right)\]

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Elastic net
\[\text{RSS} + \lambda\left({\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\alpha\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j|$}} + (1-\alpha)\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2\right)\]
The lasso part of the penalty, which is what drives coefficients to exactly zero and makes the fit sparse.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Elastic net
\[\text{RSS} + \lambda\left(\alpha\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j| + {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$(1-\alpha)\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2$}}\right)\]
The ridge part, which shrinks everything and handles correlated predictors without having to choose between them.

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
Elastic net
\[\text{RSS} + \lambda\left({\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\alpha$}}\sum_{j=1}^{p}|\beta_j| + (1-\alpha)\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2\right)\]
The mixing parameter, between 0 and 1. At \(\alpha = 1\) this is the lasso and at \(\alpha = 0\) it is ridge. It is scikit-learn’s l1_ratio, and it is tuned by cross-validation alongside \(\lambda\).

title: Lasso and elastic net
text:
When mixing helps

The lasso picks one of a group of correlated predictors and drops the rest

When \(p > n\) the lasso can select at most \(n\) predictors

The ridge part lifts both limits while the lasso part keeps the sparsity

title: Subset selection
text:
Three reasons to drop predictors

Variance: each estimated coefficient is a number with error in it

Feasibility: when \(p > n\), \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\) has no inverse

Interpretability: a model with 3 predictors can be read, one with 300 cannot




Least squares has no way to leave a predictor out. We have to do it for it.

title: Subset selection
text:
Best subset selection

Fit every model that uses some subset of the \(p\) predictors. For each size \(k\), keep the one with the smallest RSS, call it \(\mathcal{M}_k\). Then choose among \(\mathcal{M}_0, \dots, \mathcal{M}_p\) using estimated test error.



Step 2 uses training RSS and is safe, because it only ever compares models of the same size. Step 3 cannot.

title: Subset selection
text:
Training RSS is monotone

The size \(k\) winner is one of the candidates at size \(k + 1\), so the size \(k + 1\) winner can never be worse. RSS falls and \(R^2\) rises no matter what the added predictor is.



So if we picked by RSS, which model would we always choose?

title: Subset selection
text:
The cost of searching

Best subset selection over \(p\) predictors fits \(2^p\) models. At \(p = 19\) that is 524,288. At \(p = 40\) it is over a trillion.



The larger the search, the better some model looks by luck alone. Computing time is the smaller of the two problems.

title: Subset selection
text:
Forward stepwise selection

Start with no predictors. At each step, add whichever remaining predictor lowers RSS the most, and never remove one. Stop at the full model, then choose among the \(p + 1\) models along the path.



\(1 + p(p+1)/2\) fits instead of \(2^p\). At \(p = 19\), 191 instead of 524,288.

title: Subset selection
text:
Backward stepwise selection

Start with all \(p\) predictors. At each step, drop whichever one raises RSS the least. Same count of fits, same final choice among \(p + 1\) models.



Backward stepwise needs \(n > p\) to take its first step. Why does forward stepwise not?

title: Subset selection
text:
What greedy costs you

Neither stepwise procedure is guaranteed to find the best subset of a given size. Once forward stepwise adds a predictor, that predictor stays, even if a pair added later would have made it redundant.



Best subset searches everything and still overfits more. How is that consistent?

title: Subset selection
text:
Hybrid stepwise selection

Add predictors forward, and after each addition check whether any predictor already in the model has stopped earning its place, dropping it if so.



Closer to best subset than either one-directional search, at close to stepwise cost. Still no guarantee of finding the best subset.

title: Subset selection
text:
Mallow’s Cp
\[C_p = \frac{1}{n}\left({\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\text{RSS}$}} + 2 d \hat\sigma^2\right)\]
Training RSS, which falls every time a predictor is added and so cannot choose a model size on its own.

title: Subset selection
text:
Mallow’s Cp
\[C_p = \frac{1}{n}\left(\text{RSS} + {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$2 d \hat\sigma^2$}}\right)\]
The penalty. \(d\) is the number of predictors in the model, so the penalty grows every time one is added, offsetting the fall in RSS that adding it guarantees.

title: Subset selection
text:
Mallow’s Cp
\[C_p = \frac{1}{n}\left(\text{RSS} + 2 d {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\hat\sigma^2$}}\right)\]
An estimate of \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon)\), taken from the model containing all \(p\) predictors. Every model on the path is judged against that one number, which is why \(C_p\) needs \(n > p\) to exist at all.

title: Subset selection
text:
BIC
\[\text{BIC} = \frac{1}{n}\left(\text{RSS} + \log(n) d \hat\sigma^2\right)\]

title: Subset selection
text:
BIC
\[\text{BIC} = \frac{1}{n}\left(\text{RSS} + {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\log(n)$}} d \hat\sigma^2\right)\]
\(\log(n)\) replaces the 2 in \(C_p\). For any \(n\) above 7 that is larger than 2, and it keeps growing with the sample size.

title: Subset selection
text:
BIC
\[\text{BIC} = \frac{1}{n}\left(\text{RSS} + {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\log(n) d \hat\sigma^2$}}\right)\]
The whole penalty is therefore heavier than \(C_p\)’s, so BIC selects smaller models, and the gap widens as \(n\) grows.

title: Subset selection
text:
Adjusted R squared
\[\text{Adjusted } R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}/(n - d - 1)}{\text{TSS}/(n-1)}\]

title: Subset selection
text:
Adjusted R squared
\[\text{Adjusted } R^2 = 1 - \frac{{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\text{RSS}/(n - d - 1)$}}}{\text{TSS}/(n-1)}\]
RSS divided by its degrees of freedom rather than by \(n\). Adding a useless predictor lowers RSS a little and lowers \(n - d - 1\) too, so the ratio can rise, which ordinary \(R^2\) can never do.

title: Subset selection
text:
Adjusted R squared
\[\text{Adjusted } R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}/(n - d - 1)}{{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\text{TSS}/(n-1)$}}}\]
The total sum of squares \(\sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2\) over its degrees of freedom, the same denominator for every model on the path. Unlike \(C_p\) and BIC this needs no \(\hat\sigma^2\), and unlike them it is maximized rather than minimized.

title: Subset selection
text:
AIC

The Akaike information criterion penalizes the maximized log likelihood by the number of parameters. For a least squares model with normal errors, AIC is proportional to \(C_p\).



Ranking models by AIC and ranking them by \(C_p\) give the same order, so only one of the two is worth computing here.

Why cross-validation wins

\(C_p\) and BIC need \(\hat\sigma^2\) from the full model, which needs \(n > p\)

They also assume the errors behave, and cross-validation assumes nothing

Cross-validation applies to methods with no clear \(d\) at all

title: Subset selection
text:
The one standard error rule

Compute the standard error of the cross-validated error at each size. Take the smallest model whose error is within one standard error of the minimum.



When several models fit about equally well, the flat part of the curve is telling you the difference is noise. Take the simplest one on it.

Missing data

Imputation is estimation. An imputed value is a prediction, and it must be learned on the training fold.



Dropping rows discards information and biases the result

Filling with a column mean is a model, and a weak one

For prediction, missingness itself is often informative

from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor

column with that column’s median, computed only from the training fold it is fit on.

2

imputation fills the gaps, still learned from the training fold alone.

3

handle_unknown="ignore" so a category value seen in a test fold but never seen while fitting on the training fold produces all zero indicator columns instead of raising an error.

title: Pipelines and data leakage
text:
Repeated measures

Repeated measurements on the same subject are correlated with each other, not independent draws. A random split can put one subject’s rows in both the training fold and the test fold.



A nearest-neighbor model can then “recognize” the subject, since its near-duplicate points sit right there in the training data, instead of generalizing to a subject it has never seen.

title: Pipelines and data leakage
text:
GroupKFold

GroupKFold folds on the group label, not the row: every row from a given subject lands entirely in the training set or entirely in the test set, never split between them.



Pass it a groups array, one label per row, patient_id here. The fold assignment respects that label instead of splitting row by row.

Two simulations, both with 50 observations and 45 predictors. The first has 45 nonzero true coefficients. The second has 2.

def simulate(n_nonzero, n=50, p=45, magnitude=1.0, noise=4.0, seed=363):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Xs = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(n, p)), columns=[f"x{j}" for j in range(p)])
    beta = np.zeros(p)
    beta[:n_nonzero] = rng.normal(0, magnitude, n_nonzero)
    ys = Xs.values @ beta + rng.normal(0, noise, n)
    return Xs, ys


def best_of(model_name, model, param, Xs, ys):
    g = GridSearchCV(
        make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), model),
        {f"{model_name}__alpha": param},
        cv=KFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=363),
        scoring="neg_mean_squared_error",
    ).fit(Xs, ys)
    return -g.best_score_, int((g.best_estimator_[-1].coef_ != 0).sum())

title: Application exercise 9: Ridge regression
text:
Part 2: Ridge by hand
Ridge minimizes RSS plus \(\lambda\sum_j \beta_j^2\), which gives \(\hat\beta^R = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\). The predictors are standardized first and the response is centered, so no intercept is needed and no coefficient is penalized for its units.

Z = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
y_centered = y - y.mean()

lambdas = np.logspace(-2, 5, 80)
paths = np.array([
    np.linalg.solve(Z.T @ Z + lam * np.eye(Z.shape[1]), Z.T @ y_centered)
    for lam in lambdas
])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
for j, name in enumerate(X.columns):
    ax.plot(lambdas, paths[:, j], label=name)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("lambda")
ax.set_ylabel("standardized coefficient")
ax.legend(fontsize=6, ncol=2)
plt.show()










Read off the far left of the plot. What are those values, and why?

title: Cross-validation
text:
LOOCV
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\text{MSE}_i$}}\]
The MSE from the single fold where observation \(i\) was held out and every other observation trained the model.

title: Cross-validation
text:
LOOCV
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\sum_{i=1}^{n}$}}\text{MSE}_i\]
Add that leave-one-out MSE up over all \(n\) observations, since each gets a turn.

title: Cross-validation
text:
LOOCV
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\frac{1}{n}$}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\text{MSE}_i\]
Divide by \(n\) to average it, exactly like training or test MSE.

title: Cross-validation
text:
LOOCV looks expensive

With \(n\) observations we fit \(n\) models. For regression fit using least squares, there is a shortcut avoids refitting entirely.

title: Cross-validation
text:
The LOOCV shortcut
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{1 - h_i}\right)^2\]

title: Cross-validation
text:
The LOOCV shortcut
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{y_i - {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\hat{y}_i$}}}{1 - h_i}\right)^2\]
The fitted value from the single model fit on all \(n\) observations. No refitting.

title: Cross-validation
text:
The LOOCV shortcut
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{1 - {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$h_i$}}}\right)^2\]
The leverage of observation \(i\): how much that point influences its own fit. Dividing by \(1 - h_i\) inflates high-leverage residuals by exactly enough to match what leaving that point out would have given.

We’ll come back to this to define \(h_i\) in the linear regression section

title: Cross-validation
text:
Choosing k: bias

LOOCV trains on \(n - 1\) points: almost the whole data set, so almost no bias

\(k\)-fold trains on about \((k-1)n/k\) points: fewer, so a little more bias

The validation set approach trains on about half: the most bias of the three




By bias alone, LOOCV wins.

title: Cross-validation
text:
Choosing k: variance

LOOCV’s \(n\) fits are trained on nearly identical data, so their errors are highly correlated. Averaging correlated quantities does not shrink variance the way averaging independent ones does.



\(k\)-fold’s fits overlap less, so their errors correlate less, and the average is more stable. In practice \(k = 5\) or \(k = 10\) balances both.

title: Linear regression
text:
Simple linear regression
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \varepsilon\]

title: Linear regression
text:
Simple linear regression
\[Y = {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\beta_0 + \beta_1 X$}} + \varepsilon\]
The intercept and the slope, together the straight line part of the model. \(\beta_1\) is the change in \(Y\) associated with a one unit change in \(X\), and \(\beta_0\) is the value of \(Y\) when \(X\) is zero. Both are properties of the population, so we never see them.

title: Linear regression
text:
Simple linear regression
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\varepsilon$}}\]
The error term, everything about \(Y\) that \(X\) does not explain. This is the same \(\varepsilon\) from \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\) in Meeting 1, and it is still irreducible.

title: Linear regression
text:
Residuals

The fitted value is \(\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x\), where a hat means estimated from data. The residual for observation \(i\) is \[\hat{\varepsilon}_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i = y_i - \left(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i\right)\]



The residual is an estimate of what?

title: Linear regression
text:
Residual sum of squares
\[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_i\right)^2\]

title: Linear regression
text:
Residual sum of squares
\[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\left(y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_i\right)^2$}}\]
The squared residual for observation \(i\), so misses above and below the line count the same and large misses count more than small ones.

title: Linear regression
text:
Residual sum of squares
\[\text{RSS} = {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\sum_{i=1}^{n}$}}\left(y_i - \hat{\beta}_0 - \hat{\beta}_1 x_i\right)^2\]
Add it over all \(n\) observations. Least squares picks the \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) that make this total as small as possible.

text:
Stacking the observations
\[
\begin{bmatrix} Y_1 \\ Y_2 \\ \vdots \\ Y_n \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & X_1 \\ 1 & X_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & X_n \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \end{bmatrix} +
\begin{bmatrix} \varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \varepsilon_n \end{bmatrix}
\]


What are the dimensions of each of those four pieces?

title: Linear regression
text:
The linear model
\[\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\beta + \varepsilon\]

title: Linear regression
text:
The linear model
\[\mathbf{Y} = {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\mathbf{X}$}}\beta + \varepsilon\]
The design matrix: \(n\) rows, one per observation, and \(p + 1\) columns, a leading column of ones for the intercept and one column per predictor.

title: Linear regression
text:
The linear model
\[\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\beta$}} + \varepsilon\]
The vector of \(p + 1\) coefficients, the thing being estimated. \(\mathbf{Y}\) on the left is the vector of \(n\) responses, so this is the whole model for every observation at once.

title: Linear regression
text:
Setting the derivative to zero
\[\text{RSS} = \hat{\varepsilon}^T\hat{\varepsilon} = (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat\beta)^T(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat\beta)\]

\[\frac{\partial \text{RSS}}{\partial \hat\beta} = -2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y} + 2\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\hat\beta = 0\]


\[\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\hat\beta = \mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\]



Multiply both sides by \((\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\) and solve.

title: Linear regression
text:
The least squares estimate
\[\hat\beta = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\]

title: Linear regression
text:
The least squares estimate
\[\hat\beta = {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}$}}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\]
\(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\) is a \((p+1) \times (p+1)\) matrix of sums of products of the predictors with each other, and this is its inverse. If that matrix cannot be inverted there is no least squares estimate at all, which is where Meeting 9 starts.

title: Linear regression
text:
The hat matrix
\[\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X}\hat\beta = \underbrace{\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T}_{\mathbf{H}}\mathbf{y}\]


\(h_i\), the \(i\)th diagonal entry of \(\mathbf{H}\), is the leverage of observation \(i\): how much its own \(y_i\) contributes to its own \(\hat{y}_i\). It grows with the distance of \(x_i\) from \(\bar{x}\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^n h_i = p + 1\).

title: Linear regression
text:
The LOOCV shortcut
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{1 - h_i}\right)^2\]


Promised in Meeting 5. A high-leverage point pulls its own fit toward itself, so its ordinary residual understates how badly the model would have missed it. Dividing by \(1 - h_i\) corrects that by exactly the right amount.

Determinants

A square matrix has an inverse exactly when its determinant is nonzero. For a two by two matrix, \[\left|\begin{matrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{matrix}\right| = ad - bc\]



Perfect collinearity sends the determinant to exactly zero. Near collinearity sends it near zero, which is worse, because the code still runs.

Ridge regression

title: Ridge regression
text:
Ridge regression
\[{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_{ij}\right)^2$}} + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2\]
Ordinary RSS, the same quantity least squares minimizes on its own.

title: Ridge regression
text:
Ridge regression
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_{ij}\right)^2 + \lambda{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2$}}\]
The shrinkage penalty: the sum of squared coefficients, small when every \(\beta_j\) is near zero. The sum starts at \(j = 1\), so the intercept is never penalized.

title: Ridge regression
text:
Ridge regression
\[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jx_{ij}\right)^2 + {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\lambda$}}\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2\]
The tuning parameter, chosen by cross-validation. At \(\lambda = 0\) this is least squares. As \(\lambda \rightarrow \infty\) every coefficient goes to zero.

title: Ridge regression
text:
In matrix form
\[(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\beta)^T(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\beta) + \lambda\beta^T\beta\]


Differentiate with respect to \(\beta\), set it to zero, and solve. What do you get?

title: Ridge regression
text:
The ridge solution
\[\hat\beta^R = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\]

title: Ridge regression
text:
The ridge solution
\[\hat\beta^R = (\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\lambda\mathbf{I}$}})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\]
\(\mathbf{I}\) is the identity matrix, so \(\lambda\mathbf{I}\) adds \(\lambda\) to every diagonal entry of \(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}\) and nothing anywhere else.

title: Ridge regression
text:
The ridge solution
\[\hat\beta^R = {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}$}}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{y}\]
That sum is invertible for any \(\lambda > 0\), however collinear the predictors are and even when \(p > n\). Set \(\lambda = 0\) and the whole expression collapses back to the least squares estimate.

title: Ridge regression
text:
Ridge as a budget

Minimizing RSS \(+ \lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2\) is the same problem as minimizing RSS subject to \(\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2 \leq s\), for a value of \(s\) that depends on \(\lambda\).



A budget for how large the coefficients may get, spent however the fit likes. Large \(\lambda\) is a small budget.

title: Ridge regression
text:
Ridge in one dimension

With \(n = p\) and \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}\), the ridge estimate has a closed form: \[\hat\beta^R_j = \frac{\hat\beta_j}{1 + \lambda}\]



Every coefficient shrinks by the same proportion. How many of them reach exactly zero at any finite \(\lambda\)?

title: Ridge regression
text:
Variance of the ridge estimate
\[\text{Var}(\hat\beta^R) = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\]


Set \(\lambda = 0\) and compare it to \(\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}\). As \(\lambda\) grows, does this go up or down?

title: Ridge regression
text:

Ridge returns coefficients where least squares returns an error, and returns stable ones where least squares returns wild ones.



An estimate exists for every \(\lambda > 0\). What tells us which of those estimates to use?

title: Logistic regression
text:
The logistic function
\[p(X) = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1X}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1X}}\]

title: Logistic regression
text:
The logistic function
\[p(X) = \frac{{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1X}$}}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1X}}\]
The same linear function least squares used, exponentiated, so it is positive for every value of \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) and \(X\), however far the linear part runs.

title: Logistic regression
text:
The logistic function
\[p(X) = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1X}}{{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1X}$}}}\]
The denominator is the numerator plus one, so it is always the larger of the two. The ratio therefore lands strictly between 0 and 1, whatever the coefficients are.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Rearranging
\[\log\left(\frac{p(X)}{1 - p(X)}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1X\]


\(p(X) / (1 - p(X))\) are the odds, and its log is the log odds or logit. The model is linear in the log odds.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Odds

A 60% chance of rain: \(p = 0.6\), \(1 - p = 0.4\), odds \(= 0.6/0.4 = 1.5\), or 3 to 2.



Probability lives on \([0, 1]\)

Odds live on \([0, \infty)\)

Log odds live on the whole real line, which is where a linear function lives

Reading a coefficient

A one unit increase in \(X\) adds \(\beta_1\) to the log odds, and multiplies the odds by \(e^{\beta_1}\).



That is a statement about odds, not about probability. Why can we not say a one unit increase in \(X\) adds a fixed amount to \(p(X)\)?

\[\ell(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} p(x_i) \prod_{i: y_i = 0}\left(1 - p(x_i)\right)\]

title: Logistic regression

\[\ell(\beta_0, \beta_1) = {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\prod_{i: y_i = 1} p(x_i)$}} \prod_{i: y_i = 0}\left(1 - p(x_i)\right)\]
For every observation that did default, the model’s own predicted probability of defaulting. We want these large.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Maximum likelihood
\[\ell(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} p(x_i) {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\prod_{i: y_i = 0}\left(1 - p(x_i)\right)$}}\]
For every observation that did not, the model’s predicted probability of not defaulting. We want these large too. The whole product is the probability the fitted model assigns to the exact pattern of ones and zeros observed, and \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are chosen to make it as large as it goes. This plays the role RSS played for a numeric response.
